description: I'm Maryam, CS student & founder from Lahore. I learn by building and I love making complex tech simple for beginners, especially girls. Join Astro Trainer to ship a real Junior Astronaut Trainer in 48h. Looking for Frontend, Backend, Designer & Research. Beginners welcome.
summary:
We developed Lunar Kids Quest, a free browser game where children aged 7–12 become junior astronauts and run a Moon base across five missions: choosing a base, making air, growing food, surviving a real solar storm and a freezing Moon night, and finally deciding alone in Mars Mode.

It addresses the challenge by making children manage the same trade-offs real crews face. One battery must power life support, communications and science, so switching one machine on means another must wait. Children see each result as pictures and plain words, followed by a short "Did you notice?" story. Because engineering starts with math, younger players solve quick battery puzzles before powering their base. Real NASA data shapes the game: live DONKI space weather, real 2024 solar storms, Artemis I radiation research, OSDR RadLab readings and OSDR biology studies.

It is designed with Pakistani children in mind: a crew named Amina, Bilal and Zoya, a robot guide called Chandu, Urdu greetings like "Shabash", and storm times in Pakistan time, so space feels close to home.

It matters because children learn decision-making and systems thinking by feeling the consequences of their own choices, for free, on any phone or classroom projector.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Lunar Kids Quest is a free browser game where children aged 7–12 become junior astronauts and run one Moon base across five missions:

1. Find Our Moon Home: build on a sunny ridge or next to an icy crater. NASA's real plan (sunny rim, ice from the crater) earns 3 stars.

2. Save Our Oxygen: make air from water and recycle water to keep the crew alive.

3. Grow Food on the Moon: plant lamps cost power and water today, but the lettuce only arrives a month later.

4. A Moon Stay: a real NASA solar storm (move each astronaut to safety before the countdown ends) and a long, freezing Moon night.

5. Mars Mode: Mission Control is 6–44 minutes away, so children must decide alone.

In every power round, one battery has to run life support, the radio to Earth and science equipment. Before choosing, children only see how many battery cells each machine needs. After the round, they see what happened as pictures: which machines were on or off, how many cells were left, and the results in plain words (green for what they gained, red for what it cost). At the end of each mission, flashcards replay every trade-off with a short "Did you notice?" story. If a plan would leave the crew without air or water, Chandu, our robot guide, warns once, but the child still makes the decision. The base grows with the child: the site, wall, oxygen tank and greenhouse built in one mission carry into the next.

Because engineering starts with math, younger players (Explorer level, ages 7–9) solve quick battery puzzles before powering their base, and Commanders (ages 10–12) can try them too. Six optional side quests add depth: Scan the Sun (see the real NASA record behind the storm), Shelter vs Science, What if? (replay the other choice), New Mission Day, Engineer's Rewind and a Strategy Collection.

BENEFITS

- Children learn systems thinking, resource management and decision-making by feeling the consequences of their own choices, not by memorising facts.

- Real NASA science is turned into simple, playable decisions.

- Math practice is built into the mission, not added as a separate quiz.

- It's free, needs no sign-up, and works on a phone, tablet or classroom projector.

- A "For grown-ups and teachers" page explains what each mission teaches, with discussion questions for class.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want children in Pakistan, and anywhere else, to see themselves as future engineers and scientists. Many children don't have access to space-science activities, so we built something that runs in any browser, is free, and speaks to them through familiar names and words. If a child finishes a mission thinking "I gave up some water to get more air, so I need a better plan next time," they have learned how real engineers think.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- React 19, Vite 7, JavaScript, HTML and CSS

- The browser's built-in speech for read-aloud (works offline and sends nothing)

- NASA DONKI API for live space-weather data, with stored real storms as a fallback

- Vercel for hosting, GitHub for version control

- Automated tests that check the NASA data stays unchanged, that the game rules work, and that every mission can be won

- Automated accessibility checks (axe-core) on every screen

- No special hardware: any device with a web browser

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Children don't answer quizzes. They switch machines on, move astronauts to safety, and water plants one by one.

- The storm countdown uses the real time NASA's alert gave before a 2024 solar storm reached Earth.

- Choices are kept simple, and the trade-off is revealed only in the result, so the result itself is the lesson.

- Failure is kind: if supplies run out, the crew is safe and the child hears the real Apollo 13 story about why engineers try again.

- Mars Mode makes communication delay something children feel, because help arrives too late.

- It is culturally rooted: a crew named Amina, Bilal and Zoya, a robot guide called Chandu (from the Urdu word for the Moon), Urdu greetings like "Salam" and "Shabash", and storm times shown in Pakistan time.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age: two levels (Explorer 7–9, Commander 10–12), at most three meters per mission, simple words, picture results, and a Skip button on every set of flashcards.

- Honest science: every game number is marked as a NASA ratio or an estimate, every NASA card links to its source, and the game explains "How we made the numbers".

- Accessibility: large text and buttons, read-aloud, tap-to-explain words, screen-reader support and reduced-motion support.

- Safety and privacy: no accounts, ads, chat or tracking; only a nickname is saved, on the child's own device.

- Low bandwidth: works on mobile networks and keeps working with stored data if NASA's live service is slow.

- Cultural relevance for Pakistani children.

- Responsible AI use: AI-generated character images carry a visible watermark.

LANGUAGE NOTE: We use 'Shabash!' (Well done!) and 'Chalo, let's go!' (Let's go!) as encouragement buttons to make NASA feel familiar and warm for Pakistani kids. All instructional content is in English.

TEAM

Maryam, Noor and Amna.
